tasks.title: Q3: Role of Term Saturation (k1) in BM25
tasks.instructions: Study the BM25 formula and parameter explanations in Step 2 of 'src/notebooks/01-bm25.ipynb'.

question.prompt: In the BM25 formula, what is the role of parameter k1 ≈ 1.5 (Term Saturation)?

options.text: A) It removes common English stop words like 'the' and 'is'.
B) It caps the bonus of word repetitions so that keyword stuffing does not inflate scores infinitely.
C) It calculates the straight-line geometric distance between vectors.
D) It forces long documents to always receive higher scores than short documents.

question.explanation: In BM25, (k1 + 1) * TF / (TF + k1 * (1 - b + b * len/avglen)) asymptotes as TF increases, preventing keyword stuffing from dominating retrieval.

tasks.title: Q4: Vocabulary Mismatch Limitation in BM25
tasks.instructions: In Step 5 of 'src/notebooks/01-bm25.ipynb', examine why searching for 'power grid connectivity' fails to rank the GreenVolt document #1.

question.prompt: When searching for 'What technology allows devices to run without power grid connectivity?' in Cell 5, why does Doc #11 (which describes GreenVolt) fail to achieve Rank 1?

options.text: A) GreenVolt is not an edge hardware device.
B) Doc #11 is over 100 words long and was penalized to zero.
C) BM25 matches exact letter spelling; Doc #11 uses the terms 'energy-harvesting' and 'off-grid' rather than 'power grid'.
D) The BM25 algorithm ignores documents published in October 2023.

question.explanation: BM25 relies on exact lexical token matching. When queries use synonyms not present in the document text, the match score drops significantly.

tasks.title: Q8: Geometric Principle of Semantic Embeddings
tasks.instructions: Reflect on how embedding vectors represent real-world concepts geometrically in latent space.

question.prompt: Why is the cosine similarity between 'puppy' and 'dog' (~0.65) significantly higher than between 'puppy' and 'neural network' (~0.48)?

options.text: A) 'puppy' and 'dog' share more identical letters.
B) The embedding model projects texts sharing similar real-world concepts into vectors that point in nearly the same geometric direction.
C) The PCA algorithm altered their coordinates to force them together.
D) BM25 gave them identical inverse document frequencies.

question.explanation: Deep neural embedding models map semantic concepts to proximity and directional alignment in vector space.

tasks.title: Q9: Purpose of PCA Dimensionality Reduction
tasks.instructions: In Step 6 of 'src/notebooks/02-embeddings-visualization.ipynb', examine why PCA is applied before calling Plotly.

question.prompt: Why do we apply PCA (Principal Component Analysis) to reduce the vectors from 768 dimensions down to 3 dimensions before plotting in Plotly?

options.text: A) Because human visual perception is limited to 3 spatial dimensions (X, Y, Z).
B) Because Gemini vectors are inaccurate in 768 dimensions.
C) Because Plotly can only accept positive numbers.
D) To remove all numbers below zero.

question.explanation: Humans can only visualize up to 3 spatial dimensions; PCA finds the top 3 orthogonal axes of maximum variance to preserve cluster structure.

tasks.instructions: Look at the step formula in chunk_text: step = chunk_size - overlap. Calculate step when chunk_size = 40 and overlap = 10.

question.prompt: By how many words does the sliding chunk window advance forward on each step when chunk_size = 40 and overlap = 10?
question.explanation: Step size equals chunk_size - overlap = 40 - 10 = 30 words.

tasks.title: Q13: Primary Purpose of Chunk Overlap in RAG
tasks.instructions: Read the explanation on boundary loss and seam preservation in Step 3 of 'src/notebooks/03-chunking-l2-search.ipynb'.

question.prompt: What is the primary reason for including an overlap between adjacent text chunks in RAG?

options.text: A) To make the vector database store duplicate data so search becomes faster.
B) To ensure that critical facts and sentences split across chunk boundaries are not broken in half and lost.
C) To double the number of dimensions in the vector space.
D) To convert dense vectors into sparse matrices.

question.explanation: Overlap creates a buffer so sentences spanning the seam appear intact in at least one chunk, preventing retrieval failure.

tasks.title: Q14: Semantic Meaning of Euclidean (L2) Distance
tasks.instructions: Review how Euclidean distance ranks candidates in Step 5 of 'src/notebooks/03-chunking-l2-search.ipynb'.

question.prompt: When using Euclidean (L2) Distance to measure similarity between a query vector and chunk vectors, which chunk is the best semantic match?

options.text: A) The chunk with the largest distance value.
B) The chunk with distance closest to 1.0.
C) The chunk with the smallest (lowest) distance value (d=0.0 being identical).
D) The chunk with a negative distance value.

question.explanation: Euclidean distance measures geometric separation; distance 0.0 indicates identity, so smaller distances represent closer matches.

tasks.title: Q17: Complexity Benefit of HNSW Indexing
tasks.instructions: Study Step 4 in 'src/notebooks/04-chromadb-hybrid-retrieval.ipynb' explaining ChromaDB's default HNSW indexing engine.

question.prompt: Why does ChromaDB use HNSW indexing by default instead of a linear scan across all vectors in the collection?

options.text: A) HNSW traverses a multi-layer hierarchical graph in O(log N) time, bypassing 99%+ of vectors, whereas a linear scan computes distances against all N vectors in O(N) time.
B) ChromaDB deletes 90% of your documents during ingestion to save memory.
C) HNSW converts all vectors to 1-bit integers.
D) ChromaDB sends queries to external search engines.

question.explanation: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) structures vectors in layered graphs, reducing search complexity from O(N) to O(log N).

tasks.title: Q19: Role of Augmented Context Injection
tasks.instructions: Review Step 8 (Augmented Generation) in 'src/notebooks/04-chromadb-hybrid-retrieval.ipynb'.

question.prompt: In Step 8 (Augmented Generation), why do we inject the top-retrieved context chunks into the LLM prompt before calling generate_content instead of just asking the LLM the question directly?

options.text: A) To force the LLM to output binary numbers.
B) Because LLMs hallucinate or lack private/recent company knowledge; grounding the prompt in retrieved facts ensures the generated answer is strictly factual and verifiable.
C) To bypass the ChromaDB HNSW vector index.
D) To decrease the GPU memory allocated to the embedding model.

question.explanation: Standard LLMs lack private internal knowledge and can produce hallucinations; injecting retrieved context grounds the answer in factual source material.

tasks.title: Q20: LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation Methodology
tasks.instructions: Review Step 9 (LLM-as-a-Judge) in 'src/notebooks/04-chromadb-hybrid-retrieval.ipynb'.

question.prompt: In Step 9 (LLM-as-a-Judge), how does the evaluation judge determine whether the RAG system's generated response is correct?

options.text: A) It compares character counts between prompt and response.
B) It evaluates semantic and factual agreement between the generated answer and the trusted reference ground truth in answer.txt, issuing a VERDICT: CORRECT or VERDICT: INCORRECT with an explanation.
C) It checks if the response contains more than 10 words.
D) It re-runs BM25 on the query.

question.explanation: LLM-as-a-Judge compares the candidate answer against the trusted reference ground truth in answer.txt to grade factual correctness automatically with verifiable explanations.
